title: CBP Workers Allegedly Used Government Databases to Spy on Exes, Crushes, and Colleagues
gist: FOIA'd internal records covering 2009-2022 document roughly 300 allegations of CBP employees misusing law-enforcement databases for personal ends, including the first known internal DHS abuse case involving commercially purchased ad-tech location data. The insider-abuse record arrives as ICE and CBP scale spending on surveillance vendors, with roughly $515 million going to Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Palantir and Cellebrite alone taking in over $56 million in federal contracts this year.

insights.claim: Of nearly 300 data-related misconduct entries WIRED identified in CBP internal records, 78 were serious enough to be assigned to Office of Professional Responsibility criminal investigators and 138 were referred to CBP management for review.
insights.speaker: Yulia Almazova
insights.so_what: A quantified insider-abuse base rate gives regulators and litigators a concrete hook for restricting agency data access, a tail risk for vendors whose revenue depends on unrestricted federal deployment.

themes.theme: Self-querying as a corruption leading indicator

insights.claim: CBP treats employees querying their own names in law-enforcement databases as a leading indicator of future corruption, because self-queries surface early in corruption cases either as a test of whether searches are monitored or to check whether the employee is under investigation.
insights.speaker: Yulia Almazova
insights.so_what: A transferable insider-threat detection heuristic: monitor self-lookups as an early tripwire, which is exactly the behavioral-analytics feature security vendors can sell into government.
insights.quote: Historical analysis of corruption cases showed that self-querying was common across a significant number of them, pointing to it being an indicator of corruption in the future.

themes.theme: Commercial location data as the new abuse frontier

insights.claim: A DHS employee allegedly used commercially purchased ad-tech-derived location data to track several coworkers' cell phones, which appears to be the first known internal abuse case involving DHS use of commercial location-tracking software.
insights.speaker: Yulia Almazova
insights.so_what: A documented first-of-kind insider abuse of purchased telemetry is the kind of fact pattern that drives data-broker legislation and creates direct regulatory risk for location-data sellers.

insights.claim: Buying commercial telemetry lets US agencies obtain app-generated location data without a court-approved warrant, effectively circumventing Fourth Amendment protections that would apply to obtaining the same data from phone companies.
insights.speaker: Yulia Almazova
insights.so_what: The purchase loophole is the entire commercial rationale for the location-data-broker business; closing it by statute would remove the revenue line outright.

themes.theme: The vendor stack and where the money goes

insights.claim: ICE and CBP have collectively spent about $515 million on products from major tech firms including Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Palantir in recent years, on top of smaller vendor contracts.
insights.speaker: Yulia Almazova
insights.so_what: Sizes the addressable federal immigration-surveillance budget accruing to hyperscalers and Palantir, and identifies the same names as headline-risk exposures.

insights.claim: Cellebrite has contracted with ICE and CBP since 2008 and has taken in more than $56 million in federal contracts this year, with ICE and CBP securing at least 13 separate mobile-extraction contracts in 2025 alone.
insights.speaker: Yulia Almazova
insights.so_what: Concrete federal run-rate and contract cadence for a listed forensics vendor, useful for sizing the US government revenue line and its political fragility.

insights.claim: CBP's mobile-extraction toolkit spans Cellebrite, Grayshift, and Magnet Forensics, and a 2022 EPIC report showed CBP was upgrading that software to centralize data pulled from searches under active contracts then worth at least $1.29 million.
insights.speaker: Yulia Almazova
insights.so_what: Centralizing extracted phone data raises the value of the aggregate dataset and, symmetrically, the blast radius of any single insider abuse.

insights.claim: Palantir supplies both the Investigative Case Management system for Homeland Security Investigations and the FALCON analytics tool, and DHS data-sharing lets CBP agents reach much of the same data even where direct FALCON access is nominally restricted to ICE.
insights.speaker: Yulia Almazova
insights.so_what: Access controls scoped by agency are defeated by cross-agency sharing, meaning per-agency restrictions are weak protection and Palantir's effective installed footprint is larger than contract-by-contract accounting suggests.
